findings.quote:
if (!allowedKeys.has(verdict.new_issue_key!)) { skipped++; continue; }
      pushInto(byKey, verdict.new_issue_key!, verdict);
findings.claim: The scope guard checks attachments to existing issues but not the initial attachments to a new issue.
findings.whyItBreaks: If a proposal is scoped to `candidates_count > 0` and a zero-candidate row references its key, the planner still creates the issue with that verdict and the job writes the issue link. The same row would be rejected if sent to the same issue on the next run.
findings.evidence: The new-issue branch checks only `allowedKeys` before adding the verdict to `byKey`, while the existing-issue branch calls `rowSatisfiesScope` before accepting the same row.

findings.quote: const body = `${issue.body}\n\n${renderScopeBlock(issue.scope)}`;
findings.claim: Model-written issue prose can supply the first scope block and override the structured scope on the next run.
findings.whyItBreaks: When the free-form body includes an illustrative `triage-scope` block, the job puts it before the authoritative block and the parser takes the first match. A valid example silently changes routing; a malformed example makes the issue unscoped even though a valid block follows.
findings.evidence: The `createIssue` body places unsanitized `issue.body` before `renderScopeBlock(issue.scope)`, so the next run’s first-match `parseScopeBlock(i.body)` can select a prose block instead of the generated one.

findings.claim: The saturation guard does not count attachments already accepted for the same issue in the current batch.
findings.whyItBreaks: An issue with 11 post-creation rows and five qualifying verdicts passes the same check five times. The job posts all five, bringing the issue to 16 despite the configured maximum of 12.
findings.evidence: The saturation guard reads the unchanged `target.postCreationRows` for every verdict, so all five qualifying rows can be queued in `byIssue` when the starting count is 11.

findings.quote: const proved = probe?.brewery === '' || probe?.name === '';
findings.claim: An empty result from either probe satisfies the absence gate even when the other probe returned the beer.
findings.whyItBreaks: If a brewery-only query misses a misspelled brewery but the name-only query returns the exact beer under the correct brewery, a mistaken `not_on_untappd` verdict still passes. The stored class then blocks the metered web fallback despite the positive evidence.
findings.evidence: The `proved` expression accepts either empty probe even when the other returned the exact beer, and the guard comment does not say an empty result should override a positive match.

findings.quote:
if (scope.beer_ids.length > 0) return true;
  return scope.where.some((t) => t.col !== 'review_class');
findings.claim: The legality check allows whole-class scopes when a cohort is also present or when the non-class condition is a tautology.
findings.whyItBreaks: A scope with one enumerated ID and a `where` consisting only of `review_class = matcher_bug` passes, and the OR semantics admit every other `matcher_bug` row. Without IDs, adding `candidates_count >= 0` has the same effect for ordinary failure rows.
findings.evidence: The early return in `isLegalScope` lets a nonempty ID list bypass the `where` check, and that check tests only the column name, so `rowSatisfiesScope` still admits rows outside the cohort through a class-wide predicate.

findings.quote:
const parsed = ScopeSchema.safeParse(JSON.parse(m[1]));
    return parsed.success ? parsed.data : null;
findings.claim: Read-back validates scope shape but does not enforce the legality rule on existing issues.
findings.whyItBreaks: If a backfill or manual edit adds a structured block with no beer IDs and only `review_class = matcher_bug`, the parser accepts it and the existing-issue guard allows any matching verdict below the cap. The same block on a new proposal would be rejected.
findings.evidence: `parseScopeBlock` returns any `ScopeSchema`-valid block without calling `isLegalScope`, so an empty ID list with only `review_class = matcher_bug` survives read-back even though the legality check rejects it.

findings.quote: SET review_class = ?, review_note = ?, reviewed_at = ?, issue_number = ?
findings.claim: The new authoritative issue link survives the review reset that clears the class, note, and review timestamp.
findings.whyItBreaks: If a reviewed beer linked to #408 changes from zero candidates to nonzero candidates, `recordEnrichFailure` reopens it for triage without clearing `issue_number`. A query for rows linked to #408 still returns the now-unreviewed row, and if the next verdict is skipped the stale association persists.
findings.evidence: The candidate-count boundary reset in `recordEnrichFailure` clears `review_class`, `review_note`, and `reviewed_at` but leaves `issue_number` unchanged, so a reopened row retains its old issue link until another review overwrites it.

findings.quote:
`SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM enrich_failures
        WHERE issue_number = ? AND reviewed_at > ?`,
findings.claim: Saturation counts surviving review records rather than the post-creation attachments already posted to GitHub.
findings.whyItBreaks: An issue can receive 12 rows and become saturated, then a candidate-count transition clears one row's `reviewed_at` or a successful match deletes the failure row. The count drops to 11 and the issue accepts another attachment even though all 12 previous attachments remain on GitHub.
findings.evidence: `countRowsForIssue` loses previously counted attachments when `recordEnrichFailure` nulls `reviewed_at` or `clearEnrichFailure` deletes the row, while the saturation comment only explains why attachments made at issue creation are excluded.

findings.quote: WHERE issue_number = ? AND reviewed_at > ?`,
findings.claim: The timestamp comparison orders ISO strings rather than instants even though GitHub and the job use different precision.
findings.whyItBreaks: A review at `2026-08-14T10:00:00.500Z` is later than an issue created at `2026-08-14T10:00:00Z`, but SQLite sorts the review first because `.` sorts before `Z`. A genuine post-creation review in that second is omitted from the count.
findings.evidence: The raw `reviewed_at > ?` comparison sorts `2026-08-14T10:00:00.500Z` before `2026-08-14T10:00:00Z` because `.` precedes `Z`, excluding a review that occurred later.

findings.quote:
UPDATE enrich_failures
     SET issue_number = CAST(substr(review_note, instr(review_note, '→ #') + 3) AS INTEGER)
   WHERE review_note LIKE '%→ #%'
     AND CAST(substr(review_note, instr(review_note, '→ #') + 3) AS INTEGER) > 0;
findings.claim: The migration promotes the first issue-like reference anywhere in the note to the authoritative link instead of identifying the legacy attachment suffix.
findings.whyItBreaks: For `compare → #120 before filing → #347`, it stores 120 instead of the appended issue 347. It also links a quiet review whose prose mentions an issue using that notation even though the job never attached the row.
findings.evidence: Migration 23 describes an appended attachment suffix, but `instr` selects the first `→ #` anywhere in the note, so the example backfills 120 instead of 347 and a prose-only reference can also become a link.

findings.quote: const body = `${issue.body}\n\n${renderScopeBlock(issue.scope)}`;
findings.claim: Appending the scope after arbitrary-length prose can hide the routing constraint from the model while the planner still enforces it.
findings.whyItBreaks: The prompt only shows the first 2,000 characters of an open issue body. If the prose fills that budget, the model cannot see that the issue requires nonzero candidates and can repeatedly send it zero-candidate rows that the deterministic guard rejects.
findings.evidence: The body template puts the scope after unbounded prose, so it can fall outside the 2,000-character preview used by `llm.analyze` while `parseScopeBlock(i.body)` still reads it from the full body for the planner.

findings.quote:
col: { type: 'string' },
                    op: { type: 'string' },
findings.claim: The strict tool schema allows scope terms that the application schema rejects.
findings.whyItBreaks: For example, `col: 'candidates_count', op: 'contains', value: '0'` satisfies the tool schema but fails `ScopeTermSchema`. Because that schema is nested in `AnalysisSchema`, a single invalid proposal makes the whole payload fail validation rather than leaving its otherwise valid verdicts available.
findings.evidence: The tool schema accepts `contains` for `candidates_count` because `col` and `op` are unrestricted strings, but the documented scope rules allow only numeric comparisons for that column, and the required `AnalysisSchema.new_issues[].scope` makes a rejected term fail validation of the entire payload.

findings.claim: The text and nullable dispatches still fall through to an existing comparison when a new operator is added.
findings.whyItBreaks: If a later schema change adds a text operator such as `starts_with` without updating this function, the numeric exhaustiveness check and final column-group check still pass. The new operator silently matches every nonempty string rather than checking its operand.
findings.evidence: Despite the stated fail-closed guarantee, the text and nullable branches use catch-all ternaries that would silently treat a new operator as `non_empty` or `is_not_null` without reaching either exhaustiveness check.

findings.quote: verdicts: analysis.verdicts, search: deps.search, limit: probeLimit,
findings.claim: Probes and verification each get the full limit instead of sharing one search budget.
findings.whyItBreaks: With a limit of 120, 50 zero-candidate rows can make 100 probe searches and then 50 verification searches, for 150 calls against a configured cap of 120.
findings.evidence: The same `probeLimit` is passed independently to `collectTriageProbes` and later to `verifyCauses`, despite the file comment describing a shared per-run search budget.

findings.claim: Setting `TRIAGE_PROBE_LIMIT=0` does not disable the verification gate.
findings.whyItBreaks: Production still supplies `search` at limit zero, so the gate runs, marks every attachment unverified without searching, and strips references that the documented opt-out should leave alone.
findings.evidence: The verification block is guarded only by `if (deps.search)` and then drops attachments whenever `verified.get(v.beer_id)` is not truthy, while the constant comment says limit `0` disables both paths.

findings.quote: search: algoliaSearch, probeLimit: env.TRIAGE_PROBE_LIMIT,
findings.claim: The triage cron sends requests through the raw Algolia client without consulting the persistent Algolia breaker.
findings.whyItBreaks: If the breaker is already open after repeated 429s, triage still starts its probes and verification against the same service during the cooldown. The startup invocation also supplies the raw client.
findings.evidence: Both orphanTriage invocations pass `search: algoliaSearch` and `probeLimit` but no `breaker`, while the `algoliaBreaker` is only wired into refresh/enrich jobs, so triage cannot consult the persistent Algolia cooldown from this file.

findings.quote: search: algoliaSearch, probeLimit: env.TRIAGE_PROBE_LIMIT,
findings.claim: Triage enables live Algolia requests even when `UNTAPPD_LOOKUP_ENABLED` is false.
findings.whyItBreaks: An operator who turns off Untappd lookups can still trigger searches on startup during the triage window if pending rows and triage credentials exist; the cron wiring likewise does not consult the flag.
findings.evidence: Unlike `refreshOntap`, `enrichOrphans`, and `refreshTapRatings`, the cron and startup `orphanTriage` calls pass `search: algoliaSearch` without passing or checking `env.UNTAPPD_LOOKUP_ENABLED`.

findings.quote: if (!isCausal(v) || verified.get(v.beer_id)) return v;
findings.claim: Duplicate verdicts for one beer can borrow each other's verification result.
findings.whyItBreaks: If the first verdict's query fails and a later verdict for the same beer succeeds, the later result overwrites the map entry and the planner publishes the first, unverified verdict under its first-wins rule. Reversing which query succeeds can suppress a valid first verdict.
findings.evidence: Verification is applied with `verified.get(v.beer_id)`, so two verdicts for the same `beer_id` cannot retain distinct verification outcomes before planning.

findings.quote: verdicts: analysis.verdicts, search: deps.search, limit: probeLimit,
findings.claim: Verification spends its search budget on verdicts the planner will discard.
findings.whyItBreaks: With a one-search budget, an out-of-batch beer ID listed before a valid in-batch verdict can consume the only search. The planner later rejects the foreign ID, but the valid verdict has already lost its attachment.
findings.evidence: `verifyCauses` receives all `analysis.verdicts` before `planTriageActions(..., [...byId.keys()])` filters to the current batch, so foreign verdicts can consume the verification limit first.

findings.claim: Clearing references before routing validation converts invalid verdicts into persisted classifications.
findings.whyItBreaks: A matcher verdict that names both an existing issue and a new issue key should be rejected as contradictory. If verification fails first, both references are erased, the planner accepts the verdict as quiet, and the row leaves the untriaged pool.
findings.evidence: The code nulls `issue_number` and `new_issue_key` for unverified causal verdicts before calling `planTriageActions`, which prevents the planner from seeing a contradictory pair of references.

findings.quote: out.set(verdict.beer_id, resultKeys(await args.search.search(query)).has(expected));
findings.claim: Verification checks that a model-selected target exists, not that it is the orphan's beer.
findings.whyItBreaks: If the model proposes a query for an alcoholic sibling of a non-alcoholic orphan, finding that sibling passes the gate even when its ABV contradicts the shop row. The verifier has no orphan data or expected beer ID to catch the mismatch.
findings.evidence: verifyCauses derives the target solely from verdict.expected_target and checks resultKeys(await args.search.search(query)).has(expected), while VerifyCausesArgs carries no orphan row data to compare against.

findings.quote: out.set(verdict.beer_id, resultKeys(await args.search.search(query)).has(expected));
findings.claim: A successful search does not verify the claimed cause or distinguish it from an unchanged baseline.
findings.whyItBreaks: For a row whose original search already returned the right candidate, the model can repeat that same query while claiming a query-normalization bug. The gate approves the claim even though nothing about the query changed and the replay does not explain why matching failed.
findings.evidence: verifyCauses never receives or replays any original/baseline query and approves solely on resultKeys(await args.search.search(query)).has(expected).

findings.quote: const m = /\s+[—–-]\s+/.exec(expected);
findings.claim: The verifier misparses correctly formatted targets when the brewery contains a spaced dash.
findings.whyItBreaks: For brewery `North - South` and beer `Pils`, the requested target format produces `North - South — Pils`. The parser splits at the first hyphen and looks for brewery `North` and beer `South — Pils`, rejecting the real hit.
findings.evidence: expectedKey uses /\s+[—–-]\s+/.exec(expected) and slices at m.index, so it treats the first spaced dash in the brewery as the brewery/name separator.

findings.quote:
'Evidence fields for zero-candidate rows: `probe_brewery` is what Untappd returns for the BREWERY',
    'alone, `probe_name` for the NAME alone. "(no results)" means the probe RAN and Untappd holds',
    'nothing for it — strong evidence of absence; "(not run)" means no probe was made — no evidence.',
    'Use them instead of guessing: a brewery whose catalogue comes back but holds no such beer is',
    'not_on_untappd, not an alias gap; a beer found under a DIFFERENT brewery is a brewery-label',
    'problem; both empty means the beer is likely absent entirely.',
findings.claim: The prompt treats a top-three search sample as evidence about a brewery's complete catalogue.
findings.whyItBreaks: A beer can rank fourth on the brewery query and return nothing for the shop's alternate spelling. The payload omits the real hit, and the prompt tells the model to mark the beer `not_on_untappd`, which also blocks its metered fallback.
findings.evidence: The prompt states that `probe_brewery`/`probe_name` absence is “strong evidence of absence” and that “a brewery whose catalogue comes back but holds no such beer is not_on_untappd,” while `boundOrphan` only passes a rendered probe string and gives the model no warning that it may be a limited search sample rather than a complete catalogue.

findings.claim: The newly included shop style bypasses the per-field prompt length cap.
findings.whyItBreaks: An oversized scraped style is copied through `...o` in full, so an anomalous style value can bloat the entire batch or push the request over the model's input limit despite the caps on the other scraped strings.
findings.evidence: `boundOrphan` starts with `...o` and only overwrites `brewery`, `name`, URLs, `candidates_summary`, and derived probe fields, so any scraped `style` property on `UntriagedFailure` would remain uncapped despite the file’s stated per-text-field prompt cap.

findings.quote: const query = verdict.proposed_query?.trim();
findings.claim: Unbounded model-generated text is accepted as a live third-party search query.
findings.whyItBreaks: If the model puts a long excerpt from issue data into `proposed_query`, the verifier sends that text to Algolia instead of rejecting it as an implausible beer query. The corresponding failure or downgrade log can also retain the full string.
findings.evidence: query is only verdict.proposed_query?.trim() and, when truthy, is passed unchanged to args.search.search(query) and to args.onError(query, error).

findings.quote: unverified += 1;
findings.claim: The unverified digest count includes verdicts that will never be applied to the batch.
findings.whyItBreaks: If a one-row batch gets one valid verdict and ten out-of-batch verdicts whose checks fail, the digest can report one new row and ten unverified causes, even though none of those ten belongs to the batch.
findings.evidence: `unverified += 1` runs while mapping every `analysis.verdicts` entry before planning filters out non-batch IDs, and `outcome.unverified` is later set from that pre-plan count.

findings.quote: TRIAGE_PROBE_LIMIT: z.coerce.number().int().min(0).default(120),
findings.claim: A blank environment value silently selects zero rather than the default search budget.
findings.whyItBreaks: A deployment that defines `TRIAGE_PROBE_LIMIT=` coerces the empty string to zero instead of using 120. In the current wiring, that skips probes and silently suppresses all causal attachments.
findings.evidence: `TRIAGE_PROBE_LIMIT` is parsed with `z.coerce.number().int().min(0).default(120)`, and Zod's default only applies to `undefined` while `Number('')` coerces an explicitly blank environment value to `0`, which the `.min(0)` accepts.

findings.quote:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS install_usage_daily (
        date            TEXT NOT NULL,
        install_id      TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES extension_installs(install_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
        shop            TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
        match_requests  INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
        match_beers     INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
        match_misses    INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
        enrich_results  INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
        enrich_links    INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
        enrich_rejected INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
        PRIMARY KEY (date, install_id, shop)
      );
      CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_install_usage_install ON install_usage_daily (install_id);
      CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS install_registrations_daily (
        date          TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
        registrations INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
        rejected      INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
      );
      CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS match_misses (
        normalized_brewery TEXT NOT NULL,
        normalized_name    TEXT NOT NULL,
        brewery            TEXT NOT NULL,
        name               TEXT NOT NULL,
        abv                REAL,
        shop               TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
        first_seen_at      TEXT NOT NULL,
        last_seen_at       TEXT NOT NULL,
        last_seen_date     TEXT NOT NULL,
        seen_days          INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
        PRIMARY KEY (normalized_brewery, normalized_name)
      );
findings.claim: The new persistent accounting tables have attacker-controlled high-cardinality keys but no per-token row quota or retention bound, allowing a freely registered install to grow the database without limit through `/match`.
findings.whyItBreaks: After obtaining one install token, a client can repeatedly submit valid `/match` requests with a different 64-character `client.shop` each time, creating a new `install_usage_daily` row per request, and can also submit up to 200 unique missing brewery/name pairs per request to create `match_misses` rows; the 2,000-registration cap does not constrain traffic from an already-issued token, so sustained requests can exhaust disk space.
findings.evidence: Migration 52 creates `install_usage_daily` with `PRIMARY KEY (date, install_id, shop)` and `match_misses` with `PRIMARY KEY (normalized_brewery, normalized_name)` but no CHECK, quota, TTL/retention table, trigger, or bounded counter limiting distinct `shop` or missing-card keys per install.

findings.quote: date: warsawDateAndHour(new Date()).date,
findings.claim: Global API usage and the new install ledger derive their daily dates at different points in the request, so one `/match` can be split across two Warsaw days.
findings.whyItBreaks: If a request begins matching just before Warsaw midnight and finishes after midnight, `recordMatchUsage` records it on the earlier date while `recordCallerLedger` later creates a fresh `Date` and records install usage and misses on the next date, making the daily aggregates disagree for the same request.
findings.evidence: `recordMatchUsage` computes `warsawDateAndHour(new Date()).date` before the awaited cache/matching work, while `recordCallerLedger` later creates its own `const now = new Date()` and derives a separate `date` for install usage and misses.

findings.claim: All three best-effort ledger writes share one `try`, so failure of an earlier write prevents independent accounting and version updates from even being attempted.
findings.whyItBreaks: If `recordMisses` throws because its table is temporarily unavailable or a trigger rejects a row, the catch exits without calling `recordInstallUsage` or `touchInstall`; similarly, a failed usage increment suppresses the version update, causing multiple unrelated bookkeeping fields to be lost from one failure path.
findings.evidence: In `recordCallerLedger`, `recordMisses`, `recordInstallUsage`, and `touchInstall` are all inside one `try`, so any exception thrown before the later calls transfers control directly to the shared `catch`.

findings.claim: The cap alert is throttled by a fixed 24-hour interval rather than by Warsaw calendar date, so it can send twice during a 25-hour daylight-saving transition day.
findings.whyItBreaks: On Warsaw's autumn DST fallback day, an alert shortly after local midnight and another refusal more than 24 elapsed hours later but before the same local date ends both satisfy `everyMs: DAY_MS`, producing two admin alerts for one Warsaw day despite the once-per-day requirement.
findings.evidence: The cap path calls `sendThrottledAlert` with a constant `key: CAP_ALERT_KEY`, `everyMs: DAY_MS`, and `now`, while the registration cap itself is keyed to `warsawDateAndHour(now).date`, so the alert throttle is elapsed-time based rather than Warsaw-date based.

findings.quote: client: z.object({ version: z.string().max(64).optional(), shop: z.string().max(64).optional() }).optional(),
findings.claim: `client.version` accepts the empty string and can overwrite a valid stored extension version with an unusable value.
findings.whyItBreaks: A valid install request containing `"client":{"version":""}` passes this schema, after which `touchInstall` stores the empty string in `extension_installs.ext_version`; subsequent accounting reports lose the install's previously known version even though initial registration rejects empty versions.
findings.evidence: `MatchBody` defines `client.version` as `z.string().max(64).optional()` with no minimum/nonempty constraint, and `recordCallerLedger` calls `touchInstall` whenever `client?.version !== undefined`, passing the value through unchanged.

findings.claim: The CLI parses beer IDs with permissive `parseInt`, allowing malformed values to operate on a different valid beer ID.
findings.whyItBreaks: For example, `--unpin --beer 12junk` is accepted as beer ID 12 and unpins that beer's links while the output claims it operated on `12junk`; the pin path uses the same parsing pattern and can mutate or merge beer 12 unexpectedly.
findings.evidence: Both the unpin branch and pin branch pass `parseInt(beer, 10)` directly while printing or accepting the original `beer` string, so a value like `12junk` is converted to numeric beer id 12 without validation.

findings.claim: `parseBid` accepts any string ending in digits rather than restricting input to a bare bid or an Untappd beer URL.
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs such as `not-untappd.example/6614460`, `garbage6614460`, or even `-1` are accepted (the last becomes bid 1), so a mistyped or unrelated value can pin a beer to the wrong Untappd identity.
findings.evidence: `parseBid` uses `input.match(/(\d+)\/?$/)`, which captures trailing digits from any string rather than checking for either an all-numeric input or an Untappd beer URL as the comment describes.

findings.quote:
const res = pinMatch(db, parseInt(beer, 10), bid, new Date().toISOString());
    console.log(JSON.stringify(res));
findings.claim: The CLI treats `pinMatch`'s `noop` result for an unknown beer as a successful command and exits with status zero.
findings.whyItBreaks: If `--beer` contains a nonexistent ID, `pinMatch` returns `{ kind: 'noop', ... }`; the CLI merely prints it and leaves a successful exit code, so an operator or rollout script can proceed believing the requested durable pin was installed when nothing changed.
findings.evidence: After `const res = pinMatch(...)`, the CLI only `console.log(JSON.stringify(res))` and never checks `res.kind` or sets a nonzero `process.exitCode`, so any `noop` result from `pinMatch` is reported with a successful exit.

findings.quote: const recorded = recordMisses(deps.db, { at: now.toISOString(), date, shop, cards: misses });
findings.claim: The miss journal has no per-install or global storage budget, so a single self-issued token can drive sustained database growth.
findings.whyItBreaks: An install can keep submitting searched misses with distinct normalized names. Each distinct pair creates a persistent row, and deleting the install leaves those rows behind. The registration cap limits new tokens, not the number of rows a token can create.
findings.evidence: `recordCallerLedger` passes every searched miss to `recordMisses` with only `{ at, date, shop, cards }` and no install id or quota, while `MatchBody.beers` only caps a single request at 200 items.

findings.quote: const shop = client?.shop ?? '';
findings.claim: Using arbitrary client text as a shop key makes the daily usage table unbounded even for a single install.
findings.whyItBreaks: An install that supplies a different valid-length shop string on each request gets a new `(date, install_id, shop)` row every time, even for requests where every beer matches and the miss journal stays empty.
findings.evidence: `MatchBody` accepts `client.shop` as any string up to 64 characters, `const shop = client?.shop ?? ''` uses it verbatim, and `recordInstallUsage` is called for every install match request with that shop value.

findings.quote: }).immediate();
findings.claim: Registration can block the shared Node event loop waiting for SQLite's write lock, including when the quota is already exhausted.
findings.whyItBreaks: If another SQLite connection holds the write lock, the synchronous IMMEDIATE transaction waits at the normal busy timeout before it can even check the cap. If that wait expires, the capped request returns 500 instead of 429, and unrelated API and bot work has been stalled in the meantime.
findings.evidence: `registerInstall` runs the cap check inside `db.transaction(...).immediate()` and does not use the `busy_timeout = 0` pattern used by `touchInstall`, so acquiring the write transaction can synchronously wait before the capped branch is reached.

findings.quote: return db.prepare('DELETE FROM extension_installs WHERE install_id = ?').run(installId).changes === 1;
findings.claim: Self-deletion can block the shared event loop both while waiting for a write lock and while cascading through an install's usage rows.
findings.whyItBreaks: A DELETE during another connection's write transaction waits synchronously at the normal busy timeout. Once it gets the lock, an install with a large usage history must delete all of its usage rows before the API or bot can process other work.
findings.evidence: `deleteInstall` performs a synchronous `DELETE FROM extension_installs` and the function comment states this deletes usage rows by cascade, with no busy-timeout suppression or batching around the operation.

findings.quote:
key: CAP_ALERT_KEY,
        everyMs: DAY_MS,
        now,
findings.claim: The alert throttle uses a rolling 24-hour interval rather than the Warsaw calendar day used by the registration cap.
findings.whyItBreaks: If Monday reaches the cap at 23:55 and Tuesday reaches it at 09:00, the first Tuesday refusal is still in Monday's cooldown and Tuesday may get no alert. Conversely, on Warsaw's 25-hour autumn clock-change day, two refusals more than 24 hours apart can still fall on the same local date.
findings.evidence: The cap is keyed to `warsawDateAndHour(now).date` in `registerInstall`, but the alert suppression is configured only as `everyMs: DAY_MS` under a single `CAP_ALERT_KEY`, so it is a rolling 24-hour throttle rather than a Warsaw-date throttle.

findings.claim: A failure in one best-effort ledger write prevents the remaining writes from being attempted.
findings.whyItBreaks: If an INSERT trigger rejects a miss, the response still returns 200 and the aggregate request may count, but the install's request and beer counters and its reported version are skipped even though those tables are writable. Similarly, an install usage failure skips the version update.
findings.evidence: `recordMisses`, `recordInstallUsage`, and `touchInstall` are all inside one `try`, so an exception from an earlier ledger write jumps to the shared `catch` before later writes are attempted.

findings.quote:
const now = new Date();
    const date = warsawDateAndHour(now).date;
findings.claim: The per-install ledger takes its date after matching, while aggregate accounting takes its date before matching.
findings.whyItBreaks: If an install's request starts just before Warsaw midnight and matching finishes just after it, `api_usage.install_requests` credits the previous day and `install_usage_daily.match_requests` credits the next day for the same request.

findings.evidence: In `recordCallerLedger`, `recordMisses`, `recordInstallUsage`, and `touchInstall` all run inside one `try`, so an exception from the earlier `recordMisses` or `recordInstallUsage` call jumps to the shared `catch` before later ledger writes execute.

findings.quote:
const now = new Date();
    const date = warsawDateAndHour(now).date;
findings.claim: The aggregate and per-install ledgers can assign the same `/match` request to different Warsaw dates.
findings.whyItBreaks: A request counted in `api_usage` just before midnight can finish the awaited catalog and matching work after midnight, when the install ledger takes a fresh timestamp. The two daily request totals then disagree even though every write succeeded.
findings.evidence: `recordMatchUsage` computes its date with `warsawDateAndHour(new Date()).date` before the awaited cache/match work, while `recordCallerLedger` computes a new `Date` afterward for install usage.

findings.claim: The resolver reports today's date as persisted even if the last-seen write failed.
findings.whyItBreaks: If the auth-time touch fails transiently and `/match` later supplies the same version already stored, `touchInstall` can skip the second write because the principal falsely says today's date was saved. The row retains yesterday's date despite a later opportunity to update it.
findings.evidence: After `touchInstall(db, install, { date: today })` is swallowed by `catch`, the function still returns `{ kind: 'install', ...install, lastSeenDate: today }`, so the returned principal can claim today's date even when the write did not persist.

findings.quote:
db.prepare('UPDATE extension_installs SET last_seen_date = ?, ext_version = ? WHERE install_id = ?')
      .run(args.date, version, install.installId);
findings.claim: A date-only touch rewrites the version from a previously read snapshot.
findings.whyItBreaks: If two connections load the same install and one commits a new extension version before the other's date-only touch executes, the latter restores the stale version even though its caller supplied no version change.
findings.evidence: `touchInstall` derives `version` from `args.version ?? install.extVersion` and then always writes `ext_version = ?`, so an omitted version writes the possibly stale `install.extVersion` snapshot back to the row.

findings.claim: `touchInstall` reports a write even when its UPDATE affects no row.
findings.whyItBreaks: If the install is deleted after its row is loaded, passing that snapshot to `touchInstall` returns `true` when a date or version differs, although there is no row left to update.
findings.evidence: The UPDATE result from `.run(...)` is ignored and the function unconditionally reaches `return true`, despite the comment saying it returns whether a row was written.

findings.quote: client: z.object({ version: z.string().max(64).optional(), shop: z.string().max(64).optional() }).optional(),
findings.claim: `/match` can overwrite the stored version with a value that the registration endpoint rejects.
findings.whyItBreaks: An install registered with `0.23.0` can later send an empty version string, or a 33-character version, through `/match`; the ledger persists that value in `ext_version`, even though the registration schema requires 1–32 characters.
findings.evidence: `MatchBody` accepts `client.version` as `z.string().max(64).optional()` and `recordCallerLedger` passes any defined value directly to `touchInstall`, so empty strings and 33–64 character versions are not rejected in this route.

findings.quote:
INSERT INTO install_usage_daily (date, install_id, shop, match_requests, match_beers, match_misses)
      VALUES (@date, @installId, @shop, @matchRequests, @matchBeers, @matchMisses)
      ON CONFLICT(date, install_id, shop) DO UPDATE SET
        match_requests = match_requests + excluded.match_requests,
        match_beers    = match_beers    + excluded.match_beers,
        match_misses   = match_misses   + excluded.match_misses
findings.claim: Per-install accounting has no row bound per day because the client controls the shop key.
findings.whyItBreaks: When an install reports a different accepted shop value on successive requests, every request creates a new row rather than incrementing an existing counter. The string-length limit and registration cap do not bound this storage growth per install.
findings.evidence: recordInstallUsage inserts with the caller-supplied d.shop and resolves conflicts only on (date, install_id, shop), so distinct shop values for the same date and installId take the INSERT path rather than incrementing one per-install row.

findings.quote:
seen_days      = seen_days + (last_seen_date <> excluded.last_seen_date),
        last_seen_date = excluded.last_seen_date,
        last_seen_at   = excluded.last_seen_at,
        abv            = COALESCE(abv, excluded.abv)
findings.claim: The journal counts date transitions, not distinct dates, when sightings are persisted out of order.
findings.whyItBreaks: If a card's sightings are written in the order Monday, Tuesday, then a delayed Monday, `seen_days` becomes 3 instead of 2 and `last_seen_at` moves backward. The same date can then be counted again when another Tuesday sighting arrives.
findings.evidence: The UPSERT increments `seen_days` whenever the incoming `excluded.last_seen_date` differs from the currently stored `last_seen_date` and then overwrites `last_seen_date`, so an older date after a newer one is counted again despite the comment saying `seen_days` counts distinct Warsaw dates.

findings.quote:
ON CONFLICT(normalized_brewery, normalized_name) DO UPDATE SET
        seen_days      = seen_days + (last_seen_date <> excluded.last_seen_date),
        last_seen_date = excluded.last_seen_date,
        last_seen_at   = excluded.last_seen_at,
        abv            = COALESCE(abv, excluded.abv)
findings.claim: A first sighting without shop metadata permanently leaves the journal row's shop blank.
findings.whyItBreaks: If an older client first reports a miss without `client.shop`, the journal stores an empty string. A later report of the same card from a known shop updates its date but cannot fill the missing shop, unlike the backfill for initially missing ABV.
findings.evidence: The INSERT stores `shop` from `@shop` but the `ON CONFLICT` update only changes `seen_days`, `last_seen_date`, `last_seen_at`, and `abv`, so a row initially inserted with an empty shop string is never backfilled by later sightings.

findings.claim: The cap test uses the live clock for both its fixture and the later requests, so it can fail at Warsaw midnight.
findings.whyItBreaks: If `fillToCap` seeds the old date just before midnight and either request executes just after midnight, registration correctly uses the new day's allocation and returns 201 where the test expects 429.
findings.evidence: `fillToCap` inserts the cap row using `warsawDateAndHour(new Date()).date`, while the tested `/installs` requests compute their own current day later, so if the Warsaw date changes between those calls the seeded row is for yesterday and the 429 expectations can become 201.

findings.quote:
if (!allowedKeys.has(verdict.new_issue_key!)) { skipped++; continue; }
      pushInto(byKey, verdict.new_issue_key!, verdict);
findings.claim: The scope guard checks attachments to existing issues but not the initial attachments to a new issue.
findings.whyItBreaks: If a proposal is scoped to `candidates_count > 0` and a zero-candidate row references its key, the planner still creates the issue with that verdict and the job writes the issue link. The same row would be rejected if sent to the same issue on the next run.
findings.evidence: In the new-issue branch the code only checks `allowedKeys.has(verdict.new_issue_key!)` before `pushInto(byKey, ...)`, while the `rowSatisfiesScope(...)` guard exists only in the existing-issue branch.

findings.quote: const body = `${issue.body}\n\n${renderScopeBlock(issue.scope)}`;
findings.claim: Model-written issue prose can supply the first scope block and override the structured scope on the next run.
findings.whyItBreaks: When the free-form body includes an illustrative `triage-scope` block, the job puts it before the authoritative block and the parser takes the first match. A valid example silently changes routing; a malformed example makes the issue unscoped even though a valid block follows.
findings.evidence: New issue bodies are created as `${issue.body}\n\n${renderScopeBlock(issue.scope)}`, and later open issues are scoped with `parseScopeBlock(i.body)`, so any earlier scope-shaped block in `issue.body` can be parsed before the appended authoritative one.

findings.claim: The saturation guard does not count attachments already accepted for the same issue in the current batch.
findings.whyItBreaks: An issue with 11 post-creation rows and five qualifying verdicts passes the same check five times. The job posts all five, bringing the issue to 16 despite the configured maximum of 12.
findings.evidence: The saturation guard compares only `target.postCreationRows` to `MAX_ROWS_PER_ISSUE` and never adds the number of verdicts already accumulated in `byIssue` for that issue during this planning run.

findings.quote: const proved = probe?.brewery === '' || probe?.name === '';
findings.claim: An empty result from either probe satisfies the absence gate even when the other probe returned the beer.
findings.whyItBreaks: If a brewery-only query misses a misspelled brewery but the name-only query returns the exact beer under the correct brewery, a mistaken `not_on_untappd` verdict still passes. The stored class then blocks the metered web fallback despite the positive evidence.
findings.evidence: The absence proof is `probe?.brewery === '' || probe?.name === ''`, so one empty probe is sufficient even if the other probe field contains a positive result.

findings.quote:
if (scope.beer_ids.length > 0) return true;
  return scope.where.some((t) => t.col !== 'review_class');
findings.claim: The legality check allows whole-class scopes when a cohort is also present or when the non-class condition is a tautology.
findings.whyItBreaks: A scope with one enumerated ID and a `where` consisting only of `review_class = matcher_bug` passes, and the OR semantics admit every other `matcher_bug` row. Without IDs, adding `candidates_count >= 0` has the same effect for ordinary failure rows.
findings.evidence: `isLegalScope` returns true whenever `beer_ids.length > 0`, while `rowSatisfiesScope` treats `beer_ids` and `where` as OR alternatives, so an ID plus `review_class = matcher_bug` makes every row with that verdict class satisfy the scope.

findings.quote:
const parsed = ScopeSchema.safeParse(JSON.parse(m[1]));
    return parsed.success ? parsed.data : null;
findings.claim: Read-back validates scope shape but does not enforce the legality rule on existing issues.
findings.whyItBreaks: If a backfill or manual edit adds a structured block with no beer IDs and only `review_class = matcher_bug`, the parser accepts it and the existing-issue guard allows any matching verdict below the cap. The same block on a new proposal would be rejected.
findings.evidence: `parseScopeBlock` only applies `ScopeSchema.safeParse` and never calls `isLegalScope`, so a stored block with no IDs and only a `review_class` term is returned as a usable `Scope`.

findings.quote: SET review_class = ?, review_note = ?, reviewed_at = ?, issue_number = ?
findings.claim: The new authoritative issue link survives the review reset that clears the class, note, and review timestamp.
findings.whyItBreaks: If a reviewed beer linked to #408 changes from zero candidates to nonzero candidates, `recordEnrichFailure` reopens it for triage without clearing `issue_number`. A query for rows linked to #408 still returns the now-unreviewed row, and if the next verdict is skipped the stale association persists.
findings.evidence: recordEnrichFailure clears review_class, review_note, and reviewed_at when candidates_count crosses the 0↔>0 boundary, but its ON CONFLICT SET list has no corresponding reset for issue_number, while setEnrichFailureReview stores issue_number as part of the review update.

findings.quote:
`SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM enrich_failures
        WHERE issue_number = ? AND reviewed_at > ?`,
findings.claim: Saturation counts surviving review records rather than the post-creation attachments already posted to GitHub.
findings.whyItBreaks: An issue can receive 12 rows and become saturated, then a candidate-count transition clears one row's `reviewed_at` or a successful match deletes the failure row. The count drops to 11 and the issue accepts another attachment even though all 12 previous attachments remain on GitHub.
findings.evidence: countRowsForIssue derives saturation from the current enrich_failures rows with issue_number and reviewed_at, yet clearEnrichFailure deletes matched rows and recordEnrichFailure can null reviewed_at on candidate-count transitions, so previously attached GitHub rows can stop being counted.

findings.quote: WHERE issue_number = ? AND reviewed_at > ?`,
findings.claim: The timestamp comparison orders ISO strings rather than instants even though GitHub and the job use different precision.
findings.whyItBreaks: A review at `2026-08-14T10:00:00.500Z` is later than an issue created at `2026-08-14T10:00:00Z`, but SQLite sorts the review first because `.` sorts before `Z`. A genuine post-creation review in that second is omitted from the count.
findings.evidence: countRowsForIssue compares reviewed_at and sinceIso as raw TEXT via reviewed_at > ?, so differently precise ISO strings such as ...00.500Z and ...00Z are ordered lexicographically rather than by instant.

findings.quote:
UPDATE enrich_failures
     SET issue_number = CAST(substr(review_note, instr(review_note, '→ #') + 3) AS INTEGER)
   WHERE review_note LIKE '%→ #%'
     AND CAST(substr(review_note, instr(review_note, '→ #') + 3) AS INTEGER) > 0;
findings.claim: The migration promotes the first issue-like reference anywhere in the note to the authoritative link instead of identifying the legacy attachment suffix.
findings.whyItBreaks: For `compare → #120 before filing → #347`, it stores 120 instead of the appended issue 347. It also links a quiet review whose prose mentions an issue using that notation even though the job never attached the row.
findings.evidence: V23_BACKFILL_SQL uses instr(review_note, '→ #') in both SET and WHERE, which extracts after the first occurrence anywhere in review_note, while the v23 comment describes the legacy link as a free-text suffix appended by orphan-triage.

findings.quote: const body = `${issue.body}\n\n${renderScopeBlock(issue.scope)}`;
findings.claim: Appending the scope after arbitrary-length prose can hide the routing constraint from the model while the planner still enforces it.
findings.whyItBreaks: The prompt only shows the first 2,000 characters of an open issue body. If the prose fills that budget, the model cannot see that the issue requires nonzero candidates and can repeatedly send it zero-candidate rows that the deterministic guard rejects.
findings.evidence: The authoritative scope is appended after unbounded `issue.body` prose in the created GitHub body, while later planning enforces `parseScopeBlock(i.body)`, so placing the routing constraint after long prose can make it unavailable to prompt consumers that only see the body prefix.

findings.quote:
col: { type: 'string' },
                    op: { type: 'string' },
findings.claim: The strict tool schema allows scope terms that the application schema rejects.
findings.whyItBreaks: For example, `col: 'candidates_count', op: 'contains', value: '0'` satisfies the tool schema but fails `ScopeTermSchema`. Because that schema is nested in `AnalysisSchema`, a single invalid proposal makes the whole payload fail validation rather than leaving its otherwise valid verdicts available.
findings.evidence: `AnalysisSchema` validates each `new_issues[].scope` with `ScopeSchema`, but `ANALYSIS_TOOL_SCHEMA` defines `scope.where[].col` and `op` only as unconstrained `{ type: 'string' }`, so the tool can emit scope terms outside the application schema's allowed column/operator set.

findings.quote: if (!f || f.length < MIN_QUERY_TOKEN_LENGTH || BREWERY_NOISE.has(f)) continue;
findings.claim: Measuring token length after an ASCII-only fold drops genuine multi-character words from the query.
findings.whyItBreaks: With brewery `Pinta` and beer name `Øl`, `foldToken('Øl')` is `l` because `Ø` survives NFD but is removed by the ASCII filter. The query changes from `Pinta Øl` to `Pinta`, losing the entire beer name even though it has two letters. The same length check also affects brewery tokens.
findings.evidence: `foldToken` removes any character outside `[a-z0-9]` after only limited diacritic stripping, so `Øl` folds to `l` and is skipped by `f.length < MIN_QUERY_TOKEN_LENGTH` in both brewery and name token loops.

findings.claim: The new length check can miss one-character search terms embedded in punctuation-separated names.
findings.whyItBreaks: With beer name `Rock-n-Roll`, the loop sees one token whose fold is `rocknroll`, then sends the original `Rock-n-Roll` unchanged. If Algolia splits the hyphens into term boundaries, it still receives the standalone `n`, so the zero-hit failure remains for that spelling.
findings.evidence: The name loop splits only on whitespace and `/`, then checks the collapsed fold while pushing the original token, so `Rock-n-Roll` has fold `rocknroll` and is emitted unchanged with the embedded one-character `n` still present.

findings.claim: Setting TRIAGE_PROBE_LIMIT to 0 does not disable verification behavior; it marks every causal verdict unverified and strips every issue attachment.
findings.whyItBreaks: In production `deps.search` is still supplied when the configured limit is 0, so `verifyCauses(... limit: 0)` returns false for each causal verdict without searching, and this block drops all existing/new issue references instead of preserving the pre-evidence behavior promised by the configuration.
findings.evidence: The file documents `0` as disabling both evidence paths, but the verification block is guarded only by `if (deps.search)` and still rewrites every unverified causal verdict after calling `verifyCauses(... limit: probeLimit)`.

findings.claim: Cause verification receives the full probe limit again rather than the budget remaining after evidence probes, so TRIAGE_PROBE_LIMIT is not a shared per-run cap.
findings.whyItBreaks: With 50 zero-candidate rows, probes can spend 100 searches and verification can then spend up to another 50 despite a configured limit of 120, producing 150 requests and potentially exceeding the operator's intended Untappd request cap.
findings.evidence: `TRIAGE_PROBE_LIMIT_DEFAULT` is described as a shared budget, yet `probeLimit` is passed unchanged to both `collectTriageProbes` and `verifyCauses` with no accounting for searches already spent by probes.

findings.claim: Verification spends its limited search budget on foreign, duplicate, and otherwise invalid verdicts before `planTriageActions` filters them.
findings.whyItBreaks: If hallucinated out-of-batch causal verdicts appear first and consume the verification limit, valid in-batch verdicts later in the array are assigned false for budget exhaustion and have their legitimate issue attachments dropped, even though the earlier verdicts can never be published.
findings.evidence: In verifyCauses, the loop increments spent for every causal verdict with a query and parseable expected target before any publishability, batch-membership, or duplicate check, and later causal verdicts are set false once spent >= args.limit.

findings.claim: The unverified counter includes foreign and duplicate verdicts that are later discarded by the planner.
findings.whyItBreaks: A hallucinated causal verdict for an out-of-batch beer, or a second verdict for the same beer, increments `unverified` here before validation; the digest can therefore report more unverified rows than the batch actually contained or processed.
findings.evidence: `unverified += 1` runs while mapping all `analysis.verdicts`, before `planTriageActions(analysis, ..., [...byId.keys()])` and before the later `covered` calculation filters verdicts to in-batch beer IDs.

findings.claim: Parsing the expected target at the first spaced hyphen can split inside a brewery name instead of at the brewery/beer separator.
findings.whyItBreaks: For an expected target such as `Brewery - Warsaw — Beer Name`, the parser produces brewery `Brewery` and beer `Warsaw — Beer Name`; the actual result key is therefore never found and a valid cause is incorrectly downgraded as unverified.
findings.evidence: expectedKey uses /\s+[—–-]\s+/.exec(expected) and slices at m.index, so it always splits at the first spaced dash-like separator, including a hyphen inside the brewery name.

findings.claim: The new triage searches call raw Algolia search without consulting the persistent Algolia circuit breaker used by other Untappd jobs.
findings.whyItBreaks: When `algoliaBreaker` is open after repeated 403/429 responses, the daily triage still executes its probes and verification through `algoliaSearch`, issuing up to the configured budget of requests during the cooldown instead of degrading without searches and potentially extending the block.
findings.evidence: Both the cron and startup orphanTriage invocations pass `search: algoliaSearch` and `probeLimit` but no `algoliaBreaker`, while the same file passes `breaker: algoliaBreaker` to `refreshOntap` and `enrichOrphans`.

findings.claim: The planner checks scope for existing issues but does not check it for rows filed with a new issue.
findings.whyItBreaks: A zero-candidate row routed to a new issue scoped to `candidates_count > 0` passes the key check, appears in the issue's initial examples, and is recorded against that issue even though the same verdict would be rejected on the next run.
findings.evidence: In the `new_issue_key` branch the planner only checks `allowedKeys.has(verdict.new_issue_key!)` before `pushInto(byKey, ...)`, while `rowSatisfiesScope` is applied only in the existing-issue branch.

findings.claim: The saturation guard does not count rows already accepted for the same issue in the current plan.
findings.whyItBreaks: If an issue starts at 11 post-creation rows and five matching verdicts target it, all five see the same count of 11 and are accepted, bringing the issue to 16 instead of stopping at 12.
findings.evidence: The saturation guard compares only `target.postCreationRows` to `MAX_ROWS_PER_ISSUE` and never includes the number of verdicts already accumulated for that issue in `byIssue` during this loop.

findings.claim: An enumerated cohort legalizes a whole-class predicate even though the predicate can still match rows outside that cohort.
findings.whyItBreaks: A scope with `beer_ids: [1]` and `where: [{col: 'review_class', op: '=', value: 'matcher_bug'}]` passes validation, and a later `matcher_bug` row with ID 2 passes via the `where` branch. Adding one ID therefore bypasses the whole-class guard without narrowing future attachments.
findings.evidence: isLegalScope returns true solely on scope.beer_ids.length > 0, while rowSatisfiesScope separately accepts any row whose where terms all match, so a mixed beer_ids plus review_class-only where scope can match non-enumerated rows.

findings.claim: The parser trusts the first scope-looking block in the full issue body, which can come from model-authored prose rather than the structured field.
findings.whyItBreaks: The job appends the generated block after the model's Markdown. If that Markdown already contains a `triage-scope` example, the next run uses the example instead of the generated block; if the first block is malformed, the issue is treated as unscoped despite the valid block below it.
findings.evidence: parseScopeBlock uses BLOCK_RE.exec(body) once and parses m[1], so on a body with an earlier triage-scope fence it will return that block or null without considering a later valid rendered block.

findings.quote:
const parsed = ScopeSchema.safeParse(JSON.parse(m[1]));
    return parsed.success ? parsed.data : null;
findings.claim: Existing issue scopes are checked for schema validity but not for the legality required of new proposals.
findings.whyItBreaks: If a backfilled or manually edited issue gets a block whose only predicate is `review_class = matcher_bug`, the block parses successfully and every `matcher_bug` verdict can attach while the issue is below the saturation threshold.
findings.evidence: parseScopeBlock returns ScopeSchema.safeParse(...).data directly and never calls isLegalScope, so a schema-valid review_class-only scope is accepted for later rowSatisfiesScope matching.

findings.quote:
const probe = probes.get(verdict.beer_id);
      const proved = probe?.brewery === '' || probe?.name === '';
findings.claim: An empty result from one probe is treated as absence evidence even when the other probe returns the beer.
findings.whyItBreaks: If the scraped brewery spelling returns nothing but the name-only search returns the matching beer, `proved` is still true and a mistaken `not_on_untappd` verdict survives, blocking the metered web fallback for a beer the probe found.
findings.evidence: For `not_on_untappd`, `proved` is computed as `probe?.brewery === '' || probe?.name === ''`, so one empty probe is sufficient even if the other probe field is non-empty.

findings.claim: Guard counters are hidden whenever the model emits a verdict for every row, even if the planner rejects every verdict.
findings.whyItBreaks: If all 50 rows are routed to saturated issues, `covered` is still 50 because it is calculated from the model output. The run skips all 50 with no `guardHits` log, so an operator cannot see the reason for the stalled batch.
findings.evidence: The only `guardHits` log is inside `if (covered < orphans.length)`, while `covered` is computed solely from in-batch `analysis.verdicts`, so full model coverage suppresses guard-hit details even when `plan.skipped` later accounts for rejected verdicts.

findings.quote:
`SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM enrich_failures
        WHERE issue_number = ? AND reviewed_at > ?`,
findings.claim: The saturation query compares timestamp strings rather than instants.
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub can supply `2026-08-14T06:00:00Z`, while the job stores `2026-08-14T06:00:00.500Z`. The review is half a second later, but SQLite sorts `.` before `Z` and excludes it from the count.
findings.evidence: countRowsForIssue compares the TEXT values directly with `reviewed_at > ?`, and the file shows no normalization to a numeric instant before this query.

findings.quote:
UPDATE enrich_failures
     SET issue_number = CAST(substr(review_note, instr(review_note, '→ #') + 3) AS INTEGER)
   WHERE review_note LIKE '%→ #%'
     AND CAST(substr(review_note, instr(review_note, '→ #') + 3) AS INTEGER) > 0;
findings.claim: The backfill promotes the first arrow-number mention anywhere in a free-text note to the authoritative issue link.
findings.whyItBreaks: A note such as `compare alias → #12; actual gap → #347` backfills #12 even though #347 is the appended attachment suffix. A quiet note containing only an incidental arrow-number mention can likewise create a link where no attachment occurred.
findings.evidence: V23_BACKFILL_SQL uses `instr(review_note, '→ #')`, which in SQLite returns the first occurrence anywhere in `review_note`, and `review_note` is an unconstrained free-text `TEXT` column added in migration 12, so a preceding incidental `→ #12` would be cast and stored as `issue_number`.

findings.claim: The strict tool schema accepts scope terms that the runtime analysis schema rejects.
findings.whyItBreaks: A term such as `{col: 'candidates_count', op: '>', value: '0'}` is valid under the tool schema but fails `ScopeSchema`, so one tool-valid proposal can invalidate an otherwise usable analysis payload.
findings.evidence: AnalysisSchema validates new_issues.scope with ScopeSchema, but ANALYSIS_TOOL_SCHEMA defines scope.where items with unconstrained string col/op and value as string|number|null, so the tool can emit terms that the runtime scope parser rejects.

findings.quote: if (!setEnrichFailureReview(db, v.beer_id, v.review_class, note, nowIso, issueNumber)) {
findings.claim: The persisted issue link is not conditional on the row still matching the snapshot used by the scope guard.
findings.whyItBreaks: If enrichment updates a row from three candidates to zero during the LLM or GitHub await, a verdict for an issue scoped to `candidates_count > 0` can still be planned from the old row and then written onto the current row because the update only checks `beer_id`.
findings.evidence: `review()` persists by calling `setEnrichFailureReview(db, v.beer_id, v.review_class, note, nowIso, issueNumber)` after GitHub awaits, and no snapshot fields or scope predicate from the selected `orphans` row are passed or rechecked in this file.

if (!allowedKeys.has(verdict.new_issue_key!)) { skipped++; continue; }
      pushInto(byKey, verdict.new_issue_key!, verdict);
findings.claim: Verdicts can create and attach to a new issue even when their rows contradict its scope.
findings.whyItBreaks: A new issue scoped to `candidates_count > 0` can be created from a verdict for a zero-candidate row; the job then records the issue link for that row, even though the same verdict would be rejected if the issue already existed.
findings.evidence: The new-issue branch adds verdicts to `byKey` after checking only `allowedKeys`, while the existing-issue branch calls `rowSatisfiesScope` before accepting a verdict.

findings.quote: const body = `${issue.body}\n\n${renderScopeBlock(issue.scope)}`;
findings.claim: The model-authored issue body can still override or invalidate the generated scope block.
findings.whyItBreaks: If the prose includes a fenced `triage-scope` example before the appended block, the parser takes that first match: a valid example becomes the routing scope, while invalid JSON makes the issue appear unscoped.
findings.evidence: The issue creation template places model-authored `issue.body` before `renderScopeBlock(issue.scope)` without removing embedded scope fences, allowing an earlier block to shadow the generated one.

findings.claim: The saturation check ignores rows already accepted for the same issue in the current plan.
findings.whyItBreaks: An issue with 11 post-creation rows can accept all five matching verdicts in one run because every check still sees 11, leaving it at 16 instead of the cap of 12.
findings.evidence: The saturation guard compares only `target.postCreationRows` with the cap, so verdicts already queued in `byIssue` do not count toward the limit.

findings.quote: const proved = probe?.brewery === '' || probe?.name === '';

findings.claim: The new check only drops whole whitespace-delimited tokens, so one-character Algolia terms embedded in punctuation-delimited tokens remain in the query.

findings.claim: The registration response returns a reusable bearer credential without an explicit no-store directive.

findings.claim: A journal failure also skips independent per-install request accounting and version bookkeeping.
findings.whyItBreaks: If a trigger rejects inserts into `match_misses` while the other tables remain writable, a request containing a miss still returns 200 and increments aggregate API usage, but it records neither the install's request and beer counts nor its new version. A failure in `recordInstallUsage` likewise skips the version update.
findings.evidence: `recordMisses`, `recordInstallUsage`, and `touchInstall` all run sequentially inside one `try`, so an exception from an earlier write prevents the later accounting/version writes while the catch only logs.

findings.claim: The resolver reports today's date as persisted even when the last-seen write failed.
findings.whyItBreaks: If the first touch fails under write contention and the lock clears before match accounting runs, an unchanged `client.version` makes the later `touchInstall` call skip its update because the principal already says it was seen today. If there is no later request, the persisted row stays on the previous date despite the successful match.

      .run(args.date, version, install.installId);
findings.claim: A date-only touch can overwrite a version committed by another database connection.
findings.whyItBreaks: If one connection reads version `1`, another commits version `2`, and the first then touches the install without a version to advance its date, the first writes both fields from its stale snapshot and restores version `1`.

findings.whyItBreaks: If another connection deletes the install after the caller obtains its `InstallRow`, the update affects zero rows but the helper returns `true`, contrary to its documented return contract.

findings.claim: An out-of-order journal write can move the last sighting backwards and count the same Warsaw date twice.
findings.whyItBreaks: If a connection delayed around midnight writes a sighting for October 30 after another connection has written October 31, the UPSERT replaces the latest date with October 30. The next October 31 sighting increments `seen_days` again, even though only two distinct dates were observed.
findings.evidence: The UPSERT unconditionally assigns `last_seen_date = excluded.last_seen_date` while incrementing `seen_days` whenever it differs, so a later call with an older `args.date` can overwrite a newer stored date and make a subsequent newer date increment again.

findings.claim: The journal key merges distinct unmatched beers when their normalized brewery and name coincide.
findings.whyItBreaks: If a shop uses the same brewery and name for an alcohol-free variant and a full-strength variant, misses for both contribute to the same `seen_days` value and the row keeps only the first known ABV. The journal cannot tell which variant was repeatedly missed, even though the schema elsewhere documents that this card identity can differ by ABV.
findings.evidence: Migration v52 creates match_misses with an abv column but its PRIMARY KEY is only (normalized_brewery, normalized_name), while the nearby v32 beer_aliases comment and UNIQUE (brewery_text, name_text, abv_key) show shop-card identity can require ABV to distinguish variants.

    .run(warsawDateAndHour(new Date()).date, REGISTRATIONS_PER_DAY);
findings.claim: The cap-route test depends on the real clock not crossing Warsaw midnight.
findings.whyItBreaks: If the fixture fills the current day's quota just before midnight but the request is handled after midnight, the handler correctly returns 201 for the new day and the test incorrectly fails its 429 assertion.
findings.evidence: The cap test calls `fillToCap(db)`, which inserts `warsawDateAndHour(new Date()).date`, and only afterward makes `app.request('/installs', ...)` without freezing or sharing the clock, so a midnight rollover can make the seeded cap apply to a different Warsaw date than the request.

findings.quote: const recorded = recordMisses(deps.db, { at: now.toISOString(), date, shop, cards: misses });
findings.claim: The miss journal has no per-install or global storage budget, so a single self-issued token can drive sustained database growth.
findings.whyItBreaks: An install can keep submitting searched misses with distinct normalized names. Each distinct pair creates a persistent row, and deleting the install leaves those rows behind. The registration cap limits new tokens, not the number of rows a token can create.
findings.evidence: The 200-item limit applies only to a single request, and `recordCallerLedger` forwards every eligible miss to `recordMisses` without an install ID or a cumulative budget check.

findings.claim: Using arbitrary client text as a shop key makes the daily usage table unbounded even for a single install.
findings.whyItBreaks: An install that supplies a different valid-length shop string on each request gets a new `(date, install_id, shop)` row every time, even for requests where every beer matches and the miss journal stays empty.
findings.evidence: `MatchBody` limits the length but not the set of `client.shop` values, and `recordCallerLedger` passes that value unchanged as a usage key even when `recorded` is zero.

findings.claim: Registration can block the shared Node event loop waiting for SQLite's write lock, including when the quota is already exhausted.
findings.whyItBreaks: If another SQLite connection holds the write lock, the synchronous IMMEDIATE transaction waits at the normal busy timeout before it can even check the cap. If that wait expires, the capped request returns 500 instead of 429, and unrelated API and bot work has been stalled in the meantime.
findings.evidence: The synchronous `.immediate()` acquires the write lock before the callback checks the cap, so with a nonzero busy timeout even an already-capped request can block the event loop and throw before returning `capped`.

findings.quote: return db.prepare('DELETE FROM extension_installs WHERE install_id = ?').run(installId).changes === 1;
findings.claim: Self-deletion can block the shared event loop both while waiting for a write lock and while cascading through an install's usage rows.
findings.whyItBreaks: A DELETE during another connection's write transaction waits synchronously at the normal busy timeout. Once it gets the lock, an install with a large usage history must delete all of its usage rows before the API or bot can process other work.
findings.evidence: The synchronous `DELETE … .run()` can wait on a contended write lock and does not return until the documented cascade finishes; the comment explains which rows are deleted, not why that work must block the event loop.

        everyMs: DAY_MS,
        now,
findings.claim: The alert throttle uses a rolling 24-hour interval rather than the Warsaw calendar day used by the registration cap.
findings.whyItBreaks: If Monday reaches the cap at 23:55 and Tuesday reaches it at 09:00, the first Tuesday refusal is still in Monday's cooldown and Tuesday may get no alert. Conversely, on Warsaw's 25-hour autumn clock-change day, two refusals more than 24 hours apart can still fall on the same local date.
findings.evidence: Registration uses `warsawDateAndHour(now).date`, but the alert uses a fixed `CAP_ALERT_KEY` and a 24-hour `DAY_MS` cooldown, so Monday’s 23:55 alert can suppress Tuesday’s 09:00 alert after the quota has reset.

findings.claim: A failure in one best-effort ledger write prevents the remaining writes from being attempted.
findings.whyItBreaks: If an INSERT trigger rejects a miss, the response still returns 200 and the aggregate request may count, but the install's request and beer counters and its reported version are skipped even though those tables are writable. Similarly, an install usage failure skips the version update.
findings.evidence: `recordMisses`, `recordInstallUsage`, and `touchInstall` share one `try` block, so an exception in either of the first two skips the later calls even though the handler still returns the match results.

findings.quote:
const now = new Date();
    const date = warsawDateAndHour(now).date;
findings.claim: The per-install ledger takes its date after matching, while aggregate accounting takes its date before matching.
findings.whyItBreaks: If an install's request starts just before Warsaw midnight and matching finishes just after it, `api_usage.install_requests` credits the previous day and `install_usage_daily.match_requests` credits the next day for the same request.
findings.evidence: `recordMatchUsage` computes the Warsaw date before matching, while `recordCallerLedger` reads the clock again afterward, so a request that crosses Warsaw midnight can be counted on two different dates.

findings.claim: The resolver reports today's date as persisted even when the last-seen write fails.
findings.whyItBreaks: On an install's first match of the day, a busy lock can prevent the auth-time touch. If the lock clears during matching and the client reports its existing version, the route's later touch sees the fabricated current date and unchanged version and skips the write, leaving the persisted last-seen date stale.
findings.evidence: After `touchInstall` throws, the resolver preserves authentication as intended but still overwrites `lastSeenDate` with `today`, so the route’s later touch can skip the retry when the version is unchanged.

findings.claim: User-only routes can update an install's last-seen date before rejecting the install token.
findings.whyItBreaks: If an install has not used `/match` today and sends a valid token to `/enrich/result`, the resolver updates `last_seen_date` and the middleware then returns 403. Activity records therefore treat the install as seen today even though its only request was to a route it cannot use.
findings.evidence: The middleware calls `resolveBearer` with today's date before the install-token guard returns 403, allowing the last-seen update to happen before rejection; the comment explains the status code, not the update.

findings.quote:
db.prepare('UPDATE extension_installs SET last_seen_date = ?, ext_version = ? WHERE install_id = ?')
      .run(args.date, version, install.installId);
findings.claim: A date-only touch rewrites the extension version from a previously read row.
findings.whyItBreaks: With two database connections, one request can read version `1`, another can persist version `2`, and the first can then write version `1` back while trying only to update the date.
findings.evidence: When `args.version` is omitted, `touchInstall` takes the version from the previously read `install.extVersion` and writes it back in the date update, potentially overwriting a newer version.

findings.quote: return true;
findings.claim: `touchInstall` can report that a row was written when SQLite updated no rows.
findings.whyItBreaks: If another connection deletes the install after the caller reads it but before the update executes, the UPDATE affects zero rows and `touchInstall` still returns true.
findings.evidence: `touchInstall` ignores the UPDATE result's `changes` count and returns `true` even if a concurrent deletion leaves no row to update.

findings.quote:
seen_days      = seen_days + (last_seen_date <> excluded.last_seen_date),
        last_seen_date = excluded.last_seen_date,
        last_seen_at   = excluded.last_seen_at,
findings.claim: The journal overcounts distinct Warsaw dates and moves the last-seen timestamp backward when sightings arrive out of order.
findings.whyItBreaks: If a card is recorded on October 30, then October 31, then again with an October 30 timestamp after a clock correction, `seen_days` becomes 3 despite only two distinct dates, and `last_seen_at` moves back to October 30.
findings.evidence: The UPSERT compares the incoming Warsaw date only with `last_seen_date` and unconditionally overwrites `last_seen_at`, so October 30 → October 31 → October 30 counts three days rather than the documented two distinct Warsaw dates and moves the timestamp backward.

findings.quote: PRIMARY KEY (normalized_brewery, normalized_name)
findings.claim: The miss journal conflates distinct beers that share normalized brewery and name but have different ABVs.
findings.whyItBreaks: If a shop lists both a 0% beer and an alcoholic beer with identical brewery and name text, misses for both increment the same journal row. Once one ABV is stored, the other variant has no separate record, and sightings of either variant can increase the same `seen_days`.
findings.evidence: Migration 52 gives `match_misses` just one `abv` and `seen_days` per normalized brewery/name pair, so it cannot track separately the 0% and alcoholic variants that migration 32 explicitly notes can share the same shop-card text.

findings.claim: The match endpoint accepts version values that registration rejects and can use them to overwrite a valid stored version.
findings.whyItBreaks: An install registered with version `0.23.0` can send an empty `client.version`, and the route persists the empty string in place of the known version even though an empty version cannot be registered.
findings.evidence: `z.string().max(64).optional()` accepts an empty string, and the `!== undefined` guard passes it to `touchInstall` as the replacement version.

findings.quote: if (out.kind === 'ok') return c.json({ install_id: out.installId, token: raw }, 201);
findings.claim: The response that delivers the raw bearer token does not explicitly prohibit caching.
findings.whyItBreaks: If an intermediary is configured to cache successful POST responses, the registration response supplies no `Cache-Control: no-store` directive, so the credential-bearing response can be retained or replayed.
findings.evidence: The successful `c.json` branch returns the raw bearer token in the `201` response without setting `Cache-Control: no-store`, leaving it eligible for retention by an intermediary configured to cache successful POST responses.

findings.claim: The daily-cap test can fail at Warsaw midnight because it seeds and checks the quota using an unfrozen clock.
findings.whyItBreaks: If midnight falls between the seed and either request, the request uses a different date from the seeded cap and correctly returns 201, but the test expects 429.
findings.evidence: `fillToCap` seeds only the Warsaw date returned by `warsawDateAndHour(new Date())`, while both POSTs expect 429 without freezing the clock, so either request can fall on the next, uncapped day.
